grammar[1].blocks[0].title: The extra -n
grammar[1].blocks[0].text: After seit, vor and in the plural gets an -n: seit zwei Jahre*n*, vor drei Monate*n*, seit fünf Tage*n*. Not when it already has one: vor zwei Wochen.

grammar[1].fact: Germany’s national day is 3 October, the day of reunification in 1990, not 9 November, the day the Wall fell. The ninth was too heavy: it is also the date of the 1938 pogrom night.

reading.intro: You remember the postcard from the flea market: Karl, Vienna, and a certain Inge. Frau Huber has written to the address on the back. Now the answer has come, and she wants to read it somewhere with a view. She has chosen the Wall.
reading.photos[0].caption: Ein Bild auf der Mauer: Menschen ohne Gesicht.
reading.photos[1].caption: Noch ein Stück Mauer, an der Niederkirchnerstraße.
reading.en: Frau Huber: I sat here with Karl forty years ago. The Wall was still grey then. It’s been colourful since 1990. · Maya: And the letter? Is it from Inge? · Frau Huber: It came a week ago. I haven’t been able to sleep since. Read it to me, Frau Maya. I don’t have my glasses. · Maya: "Dear Frau Huber! Yes, I’ve known Karl for fifty years. A long time ago we were colleagues in Hanover for a year." · Frau Huber: I see. Colleagues. Go on. · Maya: "In 1978 he was with me in Vienna, for three days. He had a plan." · Frau Huber: A plan! Go on! · Maya: "He asked me: Inge, can you lend me three hundred marks? That was nearly fifty years ago. I’ve been waiting ever since." · Frau Huber: Three hundred marks. · Maya: "I’ll be in Berlin in two weeks. You can give me the money then. With interest. Your Inge." · Frau Huber: That’s my Karl. He never had money for cake. And I thought … · Maya: What will you do now? · Frau Huber: I’ll give it to her. And then the two of us will go for cake. She’s paying.
reading.fact: The Wall stood from 13 August 1961 to 9 November 1989: 28 years, 2 months, 27 days. Since 2018, it has been gone for longer than it stood. Almost nobody noticed that day, which may be the best thing you can say about it.

document.caption: Eine Tafel an der Brücke
document.intro: A real plaque at the Bornholmer Straße bridge, where the first crossing in the Wall opened on the night of 9 November 1989. Someone has scratched a word across it; that is part of the real thing. All of it is here: dates, a place and a sentence.
document.fact: The border guard in charge that night, Harald Jäger, had no orders. Thousands stood at his gate after a muddled press conference. At about 11:30 p.m., he opened it. Nobody fired, and the rest is on this plaque.
